questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Properties of an Elliptic Paraboloid
questions.problem: Given the elliptic paraboloid $z+13=\frac{(x-5)^{2}}{5}+\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{2}$, find its intercepts with the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the $y$-intercepts of the paraboloid, we substitute $x=0$ and $z=0$ into the equation of the paraboloid and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}0+13 & =\frac{(0-5)^{2}}{5}+\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{2} \\ 13 & =\frac{25}{5}+\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{2} \\ 13 & =5+\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{2} \\ \frac{(y+1)^{2}}{2} & =8 \\ (y+1)^{2} & =16 \\ y+1 & =\pm 4\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the solutions $y=3,-5.$ 

Therefore, the intercepts with the $y$-axis are $(0,-5,0)$ and $(0,3,0).$

questions.problem: Given the elliptic paraboloid $z+4=\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{4}$, find its intercepts with the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the $x$-intercepts of the paraboloid, we substitute $y=0$ and $z=0$ into the equation of the paraboloid and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}0+4 & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{(0-4)^{2}}{4} \\ 4 & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{16}{4} \\ 4 & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+4 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{4} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the solution $x=0$

Therefore, the intercept with the $x$-axis is $(0,0,0)$ only.

questions.problem: Find the vertex of the elliptic paraboloid $z-5=3(x-2)^{2}+2(y+1)^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The general equation of an elliptic paraboloid oriented along the $z$-axis with vertex at a point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ is 

$$
z-{z}_{0}=\frac{(x-{x}_{0})^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{(y-{y}_{0})^{2}}{{b}^{2}}.
$$

To find the vertex, we rewrite our equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-5 & =3(x-2)^{2}+2(y+1)^{2} \\ z-5 & =\frac{(x-2)^{2}}{1/3}+\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{1/2} \\ z-5 & =\frac{(x-2)^{2}}{1/3}+\frac{(y-(-1))^{2}}{1/2}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of an elliptic paraboloid that has its vertex at $(2,-1,5).$

questions.problem: Consider the elliptic paraboloid $x=\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{2}+\frac{(z+1)^{2}}{6}.$ Which of the following gives its axis of symmetry, written as an intersection of two planes?
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write our equation as 

$$
x-0=\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{2}+\frac{(z-(-1))^{2}}{6}.
$$

This gives us the equation of an elliptic paraboloid oriented along the $x$-axis that has its vertex at $(0,3,-1).$
 Since it is oriented along the $x$-axis, we conclude that its axis of symmetry is parallel to the $x$-axis.

The axis of symmetry should pass through the vertex of the paraboloid. Therefore, the equation of the axis of symmetry can be written as an intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=3 \\ z=-1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the elliptic paraboloid $z=\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{2}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{4}.$ Which of the following gives its axis of symmetry, written as an intersection of two planes?
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write our equation as 

$$
z-0=\frac{(x-(-1))^{2}}{2}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{4}.
$$

This gives us the equation of an elliptic paraboloid oriented along the $z$-axis that has its vertex at $(-1,2,0).$
 Since it is oriented along the $z$-axis, we conclude that its axis of symmetry is parallel to the $z$-axis.

The axis of symmetry should pass through the vertex of the paraboloid. Therefore, the equation of the axis of symmetry can be written as an intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-1 \\ y=2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the saddle point of the hyperbolic paraboloid $z-3=\frac{(x+2)^{2}}{2}-\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{4}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The general equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid with a saddle point at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ is 

$$
z-{z}_{0}=\frac{(x-{x}_{0})^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(y-{y}_{0})^{2}}{{b}^{2}}.
$$

To find the saddle point, we rewrite our equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-3 & =\frac{(x+2)^{2}}{2}-\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{4} \\ z-3 & =\frac{(x-(-2))^{2}}{2}-\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid with a saddle point at $(-2,4,3).$

questions.problem: Find the saddle point of the hyperbolic paraboloid $z-5=5(x-1)^{2}-3(y+4)^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The general equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid with a saddle point at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ is 

$$
z-{z}_{0}=\frac{(x-{x}_{0})^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(y-{y}_{0})^{2}}{{b}^{2}}.
$$

To find the saddle point, we rewrite our equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-5 & =5(x-1)^{2}-3(y+4)^{2} \\ z-5 & =\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{1/5}-\frac{(y+4)^{2}}{1/3} \\ z-5 & =\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{1/5}-\frac{(y-(-4))^{2}}{1/3}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid with a saddle point at $(1,-4,5).$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Properties of a Hyperbolic Paraboloid
questions.problem: Given the hyperbolic paraboloid $2(x-5)^{2}-3(y-1)^{2}=z+5$, find its intercepts with the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the $x$-intercepts of the paraboloid, we substitute $y=0$ and $z=0$ in the equation of the paraboloid:

$$
\begin{aligned}2(x-5)^{2}-3(0-1)^{2} & =0+5 \\ 2(x-5)^{2}-3 & =5 \\ 2(x-5)^{2} & =8 \\ (x-5)^{2} & =4 \\ x-5 & =\pm 2 \\ x & =5\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the solutions $x=3$ and $x=7.$

Therefore, the intercepts with the $x$-axis are $(3,0,0)$ and $(7,0,0).$

questions.problem: Find the saddle point of the hyperbolic paraboloid $z+4=\frac{(x-3)^{2}}{2}-\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The general equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid with a saddle point at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ is 

$$
z-{z}_{0}=\frac{(x-{x}_{0})^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(y-{y}_{0})^{2}}{{b}^{2}}.
$$

To find the saddle point, we rewrite our equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}z+4 & =\frac{(x-3)^{2}}{2}-\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{3} \\ z-(-4) & =\frac{(x-3)^{2}}{2}-\frac{(y-(-1))^{2}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid with a saddle point at $(3,-1,-4).$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Properties of a Hyperbolic Paraboloid
questions.problem: Given the hyperbolic paraboloid $(x-2)^{2}-2(y-4)^{2}=z+4$, find its intercepts with the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the $y$-intercepts of the paraboloid, we substitute $x=0$ and $z=0$ in the equation of the paraboloid:

$$
\begin{aligned}(0-2)^{2}-2(y-4)^{2} & =0+4 \\ 4-2(y-4)^{2} & =4 \\ 2(y-4)^{2} & =0 \\ y-4 & =0 \\ y & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the intercept with the $y$-axis is $(0,4,0).$

questions.problem: What is the trace in the $xz$-plane of the hyperbolic paraboloid $z+2=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{(y+3)^{2}}{3}?$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the trace in the $xz$-plane, we substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the paraboloid, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}z+2 & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{(0+3)^{2}}{3} \\ z+2 & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{9}{3} \\ z+2 & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-3 \\ z+5 & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2} \\ {x}^{2} & =2(z+5)\end{aligned}
$$

 

This gives us the equation of the parabola in $xz$-plane.

questions.problem: What is the trace in the $yz$-plane of the hyperbolic paraboloid $z-3=\frac{(x-5)^{2}}{5}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}?$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the trace in the $yz$-plane, we substitute $x=0$ into the equation of the paraboloid, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-3 & =\frac{(0-5)^{2}}{5}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} \\ z-3 & =\frac{25}{5}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} \\ z-3 & =5-\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} \\ z-8 & =-\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} \\ {y}^{2} & =-4(z-8)\end{aligned}
$$

 

This gives us the equation of the parabola in $yz$-plane.

questions.problem: What is the trace in the $yz$-plane of the elliptic paraboloid $z+1=\frac{(x-2)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the trace in the $yz$-plane, we substitute $x=0$ into the equation of the paraboloid, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}z+1 & =\frac{(0-2)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{3} \\ z+1 & =\frac{4}{4}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{3} \\ z+1 & =1+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{3} \\ z & =\frac{1}{3}(y-1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

This gives us the equation of the parabola in $yz$-plane.

questions.problem: What is the trace in the $xz$-plane of the elliptic paraboloid $z-1=\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the trace in the $xz$-plane, we substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the paraboloid, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-1 & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{0}^{2}}{2} \\ z-1 & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{4} \\ z & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+1\end{aligned}
$$

 

This gives us the equation of the parabola in $xz$-plane.

questions.problem: The projection of the intersection between the hyperbolic paraboloid $z=-9{x}^{2}+(y+3)^{2}$, and the plane $z=4$ onto the $xy$-plane is a hyperbola. Find the center of this hyperbola.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the intersection of the paraboloid and the plane $z=4$, we substitute $z=4$ into the equation of the paraboloid, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}-9{x}^{2}+(y+3)^{2} & =z \\ -9{x}^{2}+(y+3)^{2} & =4 \\ -\frac{9{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y+3)^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ -\frac{{x}^{2}}{4/9}+\frac{(y+3)^{2}}{4} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of a hyperbola in the $xy$-plane that has its center at $(0,-3).$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the vertex and the axis of symmetry of the elliptic paraboloid $z= 4x^2 + 8(y + 2)^2.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The general equation of an elliptic paraboloid oriented along the $z$-axis with vertex at a point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ is 

$$
z - z_0 = \dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2}.
$$

To find the vertex, we rewrite our equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-0 & =4{x}^{2}+8(y+2)^{2} \\ z-0 & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{1/4}+\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{1/8} \\ z-0 & =\frac{(x-0)^{2}}{1/4}+\frac{(y-(-2))^{2}}{1/8}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of an elliptic paraboloid oriented along the $z$-axis that has its vertex at $(0,-2,0).$  Since it is oriented along the $z$-axis, we conclude that its axis of symmetry is parallel to the $z$-axis.

The axis of symmetry should pass through the vertex of the paraboloid. Therefore, the equation of the axis of symmetry can be written as an intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=0 \\ y=-2\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the saddle point of the hyperbolic paraboloid $z+1=\dfrac{(x-1)^2}{4} - (y-2) ^2.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The general equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid with a saddle point at $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ is given by

$$
z - z_0 = \dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2}.
$$

To find the saddle point, we rewrite our equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}z+1 & =\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{4}-(y-2)^{2} \\ z-(-1) & =\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{4}-(y-2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid with a saddle point at $(1,2,-1).$

canonical_examples.problem:
The projection of the intersection between the hyperbolic paraboloid 

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{4} - \dfrac{(y+5) ^2}{3} = z-1
$$

and the plane $x=2$  onto the $yz$-plane is a parabola. Find the vertex of this parabola.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the intersection of the paraboloid and the plane $x=2,$ we substitute $x=2$ into the equation of the paraboloid and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}-\frac{(y+5)^{2}}{3} & =z-1 \\ \frac{{2}^{2}}{4}-\frac{(y+5)^{2}}{3} & =z-1 \\ 1-\frac{(y+5)^{2}}{3} & =z-1 \\ z & =-\frac{1}{3}(y+5)^{2}+2\end{aligned}
$$

Projecting this onto the $yz$-plane, we get the equation of a parabola that has its vertex at $(-5,2).$
